clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Recommend Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) x3-4 vessels over Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) based on FREEDOM and SYNTAX clinical trial evidence demonstrating superior long-term survival and reduced myocardial infarction/revascularization rates in diabetic multi-vessel disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe crushing chest pain, triple-vessel coronary artery disease on angiogram, and diabetes requiring bypass evaluation

Key HPI features: 62M with type 2 diabetes admitted to cardiac care unit with unstable angina. Coronary angiography performed yesterday revealed severe multi-vessel coronary artery disease: 90% proximal left anterior descending (LAD) stenosis, 85% circumflex artery stenosis, and 95% right coronary artery (RCA) stenosis with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (40%). Interventional cardiology requested cardiothoracic surgery consultation for surgical revascularization.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 66, BP 128/78. Chest clear to auscultation. SYNTAX score calculated from angiogram is 34 (high anatomical complexity). LVEF 40% with anterior hypokinesis. Allen test confirms patent palmar arch of left arm suitable for radial artery harvest. Bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler confirms great saphenous veins patent without varicosities.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (insulin-requiring), Hypertension, CAD
Current medications: Insulin glargine 30 units QHS, Aspirin 81mg, Atorvastatin 80mg, Metoprolol 50mg BID
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Single/double-vessel disease (would favor PCI) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Ongoing rest angina — suggests unstable disease needing urgent revascularization.
management_principles: Recommend Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) x3-4 vessels over Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) based on FREEDOM and SYNTAX clinical trial evidence demonstrating superior long-term survival and reduced myocardial infarction/revascularization rates in diabetic multi-vessel disease
Surgical plan: Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA) to LAD (gold standard for long-term patency), plus saphenous vein/radial artery grafts to circumflex and RCA targets
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: severe crushing chest pain, triple-vessel coronary artery disease on angiogram, and diabetes requiring bypass evaluation

62M with type 2 diabetes admitted to cardiac care unit with unstable angina. Coronary angiography performed yesterday revealed severe multi-vessel coronary artery disease: 90% proximal left anterior descending (LAD) stenosis, 85% circumflex artery stenosis, and 95% right coronary artery (RCA) stenosis with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (40%). Interventional cardiology requested cardiothoracic surgery consultation for surgical revascularization.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 66, BP 128/78. Chest clear to auscultation. SYNTAX score calculated from angiogram is 34 (high anatomical complexity). LVEF 40% with anterior hypokinesis. Allen test confirms patent palmar arch of left arm suitable for radial artery harvest. Bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler confirms great saphenous veins patent without varicosities.
reference_soap.assessment: Severe Three-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease in an insulin-dependent diabetic patient with reduced LVEF (SYNTAX score > 33).
reference_soap.plan: Recommend Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) x3-4 vessels over Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) based on FREEDOM and SYNTAX clinical trial evidence demonstrating superior long-term survival and reduced myocardial infarction/revascularization rates in diabetic multi-vessel disease. Surgical plan: Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA) to LAD (gold standard for long-term patency), plus saphenous vein/radial artery grafts to circumflex and RCA targets.

learning_objectives: Explain evidence-based guidelines (FREEDOM and SYNTAX trials) favoring CABG over PCI in diabetic patients with multivessel coronary disease and complex anatomy
Understand the superior long-term patency rates and survival benefit of using the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA) grafted to the LAD artery over venous conduits
Perform pre-operative assessment of conduit vessels (radial artery Allen test, great saphenous vein evaluation)
Outline perioperative management of glycemic control, antiplatelet therapy, and renal protection during cardiac surgery

teaching.one_liner: Severe blockages in all three major coronary arteries, especially in a diabetic patient with reduced heart pumping function, where bypass surgery has a proven survival advantage over stenting.
red_flags: Ongoing rest angina — suggests unstable disease needing urgent revascularization

must_ask.say: How severe is your chest pain, and does it happen with minimal activity now?
How long have you had diabetes, and is it insulin-dependent?
Have you had a stent or angiogram before?
What worries you about having open heart surgery instead of stents?
How far can you walk before the chest pain starts?

history.answer: I was admitted two days ago after having severe crushing chest pain, and the doctors told me my angiogram showed blockages in three main arteries.
The severe pain started suddenly two evenings ago while I was watching television on the couch.
It felt like a heavy weight pressing directly on the middle of my chest, behind my breastbone.
It was a tight, crushing pressure, like an elephant was stepping right on my chest.
The tightness spread up into my neck, my lower jaw, and down the inside of my left arm.
That severe attack lasted about twenty-five minutes until the paramedics gave me nitroglycerin and oxygen.
It was an eight or nine out of ten when it peaked at home, much worse than the mild tightness I used to feel.
For the past month I had mild tightness when climbing stairs that stopped with rest, but this severe episode came on completely at rest.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or changing my position did not change the pain at all, and pressing on my chest did not make it worse.
It was not related to eating or spicy foods, and I did not have any sour acid backing up into my throat or pain swallowing.
I broke out in a heavy cold sweat and felt quite short of breath and nauseated, but I did not vomit or pass out.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I have been feeling completely well otherwise with no cold, sore throat, or body aches recently.
No, neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I have not been on any long flights or immobilized in bed before this.
No, there have been no rashes, blisters, or skin spots on my chest.
I was terrified that I was having a fatal heart attack during the episode, but I did not have tingling in my hands or feet.
I have had type 2 diabetes for twelve years and high blood pressure for ten years, but my cholesterol has been treated with medication.
I have had mild exertional chest tightness for a few weeks, but never pain this bad, and I have never had stents or a heart catheterization before yesterday.
No, I have had no blows, falls, heavy lifting, or injuries to my chest wall.
I've had diabetes for twelve years; I currently take a long-acting insulin injection every night, and my doctor keeps a close eye on my blood sugar.
Before this past month, I could walk briskly on flat ground for thirty minutes without trouble, but lately climbing more than one flight of stairs brought on chest tightness.
I was really hoping they could just put in stents because that seems much easier and less invasive than opening up my chest.
I am very nervous about being put on a heart-lung bypass machine and having my breastbone cracked open and healing afterward.
I want a clear explanation of why open bypass surgery would be better or safer for me than getting stents.
I have type 2 diabetes mellitus, high blood pressure, and coronary artery disease.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty-two, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations until this admission.
I take insulin glargine thirty units at bedtime, aspirin 81 milligrams, atorvastatin 80 milligrams daily, and metoprolol 50 milligrams twice a day.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or iodine dye.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vape products.
I have a glass of red wine on special occasions maybe once a month, but I don't drink regularly.
I work as an accountant and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father had a heart attack in his late fifties and had bypass surgery, and my mother had high blood pressure.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, pulse 66 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Comfortable at rest in bed, alert, no diaphoresis, pallor, or acute distress.
No jugular venous distension observed with the head elevated at 45 degrees.
No skin rash, vesicles, bruising, or superficial lesions over the chest wall.
No chest wall tenderness or reproducible pain on palpation of costochondral junctions and ribs.
Resonant percussion notes symmetrically across all lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rub.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, no heart murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender to light and deep palpation, without epigastric tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly.
No bilateral pedal or pretibial edema; great saphenous veins are soft and non-varicose bilaterally.
Calves are symmetrical, supple, non-tender, without cords or warmth.
Radial and pedal pulses are intact and symmetrical; modified Allen test shows prompt palmar collateral refill in the left hand within 5 seconds.
